newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia will meet EMU criteria by 2001 - premier.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia will meet EMU criteria by 2001 - premier.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said on Thursday the country would meet the criteria of European economic and monetary union before its planned entry into the EU by 2001.
He predicted that inflation, currently at around nine percent, would drop to three percent within the next two to three years.
"Slovenia can realistically decrease its inflation rate to three percent within the next two to three years," Drnovsek told Reuters in an interview.

Drnovsek said the speed at which the inflation rate would decrease depended largely on the restructuring of energy prices in the former Yugoslav republic, which are significantly lower than in the European Union.
"If we do all of the adjustment next year, inflation in 1997 would be between eight and nine percent, whereas it could drop to six percent if we decide on a gradual adjustment," Drnovsek said.

Drnovsek's coalition government faces a general election on November 10. The Alpine republic signed an association agreement with the EU in June and formally applied for membership of the bloc it hopes to join by 2001.
Despite Slovenia's economic strength, exporters have complained that the high value of the Slovenian currency, the tolar, is hurting growth and putting pressure on their companies.
"I think the strength of the tolar is becoming a problem for our exporters," Drnovsek said.
He said the central bank had tried to influence the tolar rate to make it more acceptable to exporters but added: "These are only very slight movements."
"I do not expect a sudden devaluation," he said.
The tolar was quoted at 90.2 to the German mark on Thursday, compared to 88.0 at the start of the year.
In an address to an international economic conference in Bled, Drnovsek stressed that Slovenia enjoyed the confidence of international investors and institutions.
"Our issue of Eurobonds was very successful and was met by large interest from investors," he told some 200 delegates at the conference at a lakeside hotel.

He said Slovenia's success lay in agreements with commercial bank creditors of the former Yugoslavia. The agreement, finalised in June, meant that Slovenia took over 18 percent of the $4.3 billion of commercial debt of the ex-Yugoslav federation.
